p.x:
Last week was a bad week for me. I had three exams, and I felt very tired. I couldn't sleep well because I was always thinking about my grades. I didn't want to see my friends, and I spent a lot of time alone in my room.
On Friday, my best friend Fon asked me, "Are you OK? You look worried." At first, I said I was fine. But then I told her about my feelings. She listened and said, "Don't worry. Everyone feels like this sometimes."
Fon taught me to breathe slowly when I feel stressed. She also told me to take a rest and go for a walk. Now I feel much better. I learned that talking to someone is good for you.

We all know how to look after our bodies: eat well, exercise and sleep. But our minds need care too. Many young people feel anxious about exams, friendships or the future, and loneliness is becoming more common, even among people with hundreds of online friends.
It's important to notice the signs that someone is struggling. They may stop doing things they enjoy, sleep too much or too little, or become very quiet. If you notice these signs in a friend, ask gently how they are. Sometimes people need time to open up.
There are many simple ways to improve your mental health. Some people write in a journal every evening, which helps them understand their thoughts. Others find that sport, art or music builds their confidence.
If feelings of sadness or worry continue for a long time, it's a good idea to talk to a professional. Many schools and universities have a counsellor, and therapy can help people understand and manage their emotions. In Thailand, you can also call the Department of Mental Health helpline on 1323 for free, confidential support.

For generations, mental illness was a taboo subject in many societies, including Thailand. People who suffered from depression or anxiety often hid their symptoms out of fear of being judged, and the stigma attached to seeing a psychiatrist or psychologist prevented many from seeking help. Today, attitudes are changing, but slowly.
Mental health conditions are extremely common. The World Health Organization estimates that around one in eight people worldwide lives with a mental disorder. Experiences such as trauma, grief, chronic stress and, among young people, intense peer pressure and social media comparison can all contribute. Symptoms vary widely: one person may experience a sudden panic attack, while another may gradually lose interest in life and begin to isolate themselves.
Effective treatment is available. A professional can diagnose the condition and recommend an appropriate approach, which may include talking therapy with a therapist, medication, or a combination of the two. Recovery is not always a straight line; a relapse does not mean failure, and ongoing support makes a significant difference.
Alongside professional care, everyday habits matter. Research supports practices such as mindfulness, regular exercise, keeping a gratitude diary and setting healthy boundaries with work and technology. Self-care, however, is not a substitute for treatment when it is needed. Perhaps the most powerful change of all is cultural: when families, schools and workplaces respond to people's difficulties in a compassionate rather than critical way, self-esteem is protected and people are far more likely to ask for help early.
